newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lagerfeld tough-girl look tops off Paris season.
newsitem.headline: Lagerfeld tough-girl look tops off Paris season.

text.p: German designer Karl Lagerfeld unleashed clothes for tough, street-wise girls in his signature collection on Monday, topping off eight days of Autumn-Winter ready-to-wear collections by Paris's major fashion houses.

"It's about modern women, modern clothes, modern material, modern proportions, and cut and detailing. At the same time it's very minimalist, you have to look twice to see how elaborate the craftsmanship is," Lagerfeld told reporters backstage.
"It's for a quite aggressive woman with high heels, but a very liberated woman. It's not about long and short, it's about lean silhouettes, lean bodies and freedom," he added.

Models with greasy hair sported tattered fur stoles over wispy slip dress and stiletto heels, conjuring up images of speed-popping night club queens at rave parties. This was highlighted by the pounding rhythm of techno music.

There were shiny snakeskins, coats of tiger print or crocodile and leopard patchwork, and swollen shoulders on skinny leather-clad limbs recalling the hair-raising creatures in Tim Burton's science fiction film "Mars Attacks".

As Lagerfeld left the catwalk after taking his bows, a militant from People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) leapt on stage waving one of the designer's jackets with "Fur is dead" scrawled on the back.

The honorary final slot of a fashion season -- other minor designers will continue to stage their collections through Wednesday -- is traditionally given to one of the most highly regarded designers, but this collection was an anti-climax.
The ready-to-wear season was characterised by soul-searching among Paris designers struggling with a weak domestic economy.

"France has a lot of problems right now and the economic crisis still has not been absorbed. People don't want to give free rein to their imaginations," said Claire Perrin, a buyer for France's Galeries Lafayette department store.
"The economic atmosphere is not favourable to creation and people are asking designers to make clothes that sell," she added.
The major trends for next winter will be in the colours -- purples from aubergine through plum to lavender, deep browns like chocolate and cocoa and bordeaux.

Flamboyant ethnic influence from Asia, mainly China and Japan, but also Tibet and Afghanistan at Dries Van Noten, and Russia at Chanel and Kenzo, were a key thread during these last eight days, and were often presented with austere men's suiting.
Animal skins, from snake to panther and crocodile, figured strongly at shows by Alexander McQueen for Givenchy, John Galliano, Emanuel Ungaro, Lagerfeld and Galliano's collection for Christian Dior.

Fur was also back in full force at many of those labels as well as several others, including Lolita Lempicka, Kenzo and Bertrand Marechal -- who showed a long white mink on a stark naked model -- despite protests by animals' rights activists.

The 1980s power look was less prevalent than pre-season rumours had announced, but Chanel, Givenchy and Brazilian designer Ocimar Versolato gave it a nod, while tartan plaids and mohair sewaters and dresses made a strong showing.
Other trends included stiletto heels, patterned hose and sandals for winter.
